name: Tooth filing / enamel shaving DIY
lead: Tooth filing or enamel shaving at home is the practice of using a file, sanding tool or similar abrasive to alter the shape, length or shade of one's own teeth without a dentist. Participants in appearance forums discuss it as a way to even out edges or lighten teeth.

Dentists perform a supervised version called odontoplasty, enameloplasty or contouring, which reshapes teeth by removing part of the enamel.[5] Enamel does not regenerate, so removal is permanent.[3][5]
No studies of do-it-yourself enamel removal were found. This article describes the practice and what dental sources report about enamel and professional contouring, and does not give instructions.

paras: Home enamel removal involves abrasive tools applied to the teeth to change shape, smooth chips, or attempt shade change. Its professional counterpart, odontoplasty, can repair a small chip or alter the length, shape or position of a tooth, and is sometimes described as an alternative to braces in selected cases.[5]

Enamel is about 96 percent mineral and contains no cells, blood vessels or nerves; the cells that formed it are lost before the tooth erupts, so the body cannot regenerate it.[3] Remineralisation can repair some early damage, but dentists cannot restore lost enamel.[3] It is thickest at the cusps, up to about 2.5 mm, and thinner near the gumline.[3] Normal wear is estimated at about 8 micrometres per year.[3]

Dentists who contour teeth note that removal is permanent and may sometimes expose dentin.[5] Dental polishing, a routine office procedure, is reported to remove about one micron of enamel per treatment, a far smaller amount.[2][6]

Dental sources describe loss of enamel and exposure of dentin as risks of enamel removal.[5] Tooth wear literature describes progressive wear exposing dentine, and in severe cases the pulp.[4] Enamel left without dentin underneath is described as more prone to fracture.[3] Because stains inside a tooth originate in dentin or enamel structure, abrasion of the surface does not change intrinsic colour.[1][2]

card.summary: Home filing or sanding of teeth for shape or shade; dentists describe enamel loss as permanent and no studies exist.
card.note: Enamel cannot regenerate; dental sources describe dentin exposure as a risk.

quick.overview:
This is the practice of abrading or filing one's own teeth at home to change shape or lighten them. A dentist-performed version exists and is called odontoplasty or contouring.

No studies of the DIY version were found.
quick.mechanism: Abrasive tools physically remove enamel. Because enamel has no cells and does not regrow, the change is permanent.
quick.risks: Dental sources describe permanent enamel loss, possible dentin exposure and greater fracture risk in thinned enamel. No safety data exist for unsupervised home use.
